instructions: Cut 4 of the green onions in half crosswise. Slice the 2-inch piece of ginger into thin coins and split them into two piles.

Pat the pork belly dry with paper towels. Heat the 1/2 tbsp oil in a heavy skillet over medium-high until it shimmers. Lay in the pork fat side down and cook for 2 to 3 minutes without moving it, until it's golden brown. Stand back a little. It spatters.
Turn the pork and brown each of the other sides the same way, about 2 minutes each.
Transfer the pork to a large pot. Add the halved green onions, one pile of the ginger and 1/4 cup of the sake. Pour in cold water to cover the pork by about 1 inch.
Bring it to a boil over medium-high. Skim off the gray foam that rises to the top with a spoon.

Turn the heat down to low so the water barely bubbles. Cut a circle of parchment paper a little smaller than the pot, snip a small hole in the middle and lay it right on the water. Simmer for 3 hours. Check it every 30 minutes and pour in hot water whenever the pork starts to poke out.

About 30 minutes before the 3 hours are up, bring a small pot of water to a boil. Add the 1/4 lb snap peas and cook them for 1 1/2 to 2 minutes, until they're bright green. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and rinse them under cold water.

Turn the heat under the small pot down to medium-low. Gently lower in the 4 eggs and cook them for 7 minutes. Transfer them to a bowl of cold water, leave them until they're cool enough to hold, then peel them.
When the 3 hours are up, lift the pork onto a board and throw out the cooking water and aromatics. Let the pork cool for 5 minutes, then cut it into 2-inch cubes.

Rinse out the pot. Off the heat, stir the 1 1/4 tsp dashi granules into 2 1/2 cups water in it. Add the pork cubes, the last 1/4 cup sake, the 1/4 cup mirin, the 1/4 cup sugar and the other pile of ginger.
Bring it to a simmer over medium, then turn the heat down to low. Lay the parchment circle back on top and simmer for 30 minutes.
Meanwhile, rinse the 1 1/2 cups rice in cold water until the water runs mostly clear, then cook it in a rice cooker or a covered pot.

Stir the 1/4 cup soy sauce into the pot and add the peeled eggs. Put the parchment back and simmer on low for 30 minutes, turning the eggs now and then so they color evenly. It's ready when the pork is tender enough to cut with a spoon and the liquid has cooked down by about half. Keep the heat low so the pot doesn't boil dry.
Thinly slice the last 2 green onions. Cut the snap peas in half on an angle.
Taste the sauce. If it's flat, add a splash of soy sauce.

Cut the eggs in half. Put the pork in bowls with the eggs and snap peas, spoon some of the braising liquid over and scatter the green onions on top. Serve with the rice, with the shichimi togarashi at the table.
method_notes: Both versions boil the pork belly in plain water first, then braise cubes of it in dashi, sake, soy sauce and sugar with ginger, add soft-boiled eggs near the end and serve it with rice and mustard or chili on the side. Just One Cookbook, the lead, sears the block first, boils it for 3 hours with green onion, ginger and sake under a drop lid, and braises the cubes for an hour with mirin, adding the soy sauce halfway. Norecipes boils the pork for only 30 minutes, braises it for up to 2 hours with garlic and dark brown sugar and rests it overnight before glazing it in the reduced sauce. This one follows the lead's timings and ratios with instant dashi, keeps the snap peas and shichimi togarashi the lead serves it with, and leaves out the lead's optional dried chili so the pot stays mild. Both sources say it tastes even better if the pork cools in its liquid for a few hours or overnight and is warmed through gently.
